title: Imperfect and future

objectives.can: Recognise imperfect and future indicatives and parse them.

explanation.summary: Latin marks the imperfect and the future by a tense sign placed between the stem and the personal endings you already know. The imperfect describes a past action as going on or repeated; the future looks forward. Both are very common in the Gospels.

sections.heading: The imperfect: -ba-
body: The imperfect adds -ba- to the present stem, and then the personal endings: -m for 'I', and -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt for the others. The vowel before -ba- belongs to the conjugation: -a- in the first (*laudabat*), -e- in the second and third (*habebat*, *dicebat*), -ie- in the fourth and in the third conjugation -io verbs (*audiebat*, *faciebat*).

The imperfect presents a past action as unfinished: going on at the time, repeated, or customary. In Mark 6:20 *audiebat* is rendered 'he used to listen' or 'he would listen', because Herod did this on more than one occasion. The perfect (taught later in this unit) names the action as a completed whole. The two are not the same as English tenses: the imperfect may be translated 'was doing', 'used to do', 'kept doing' or just 'did', depending on the sentence.

sections.heading: The future: two patterns
body: The first and second conjugations form the future with -bo, -bi-, -bu-: the tense sign is -b-, followed by the vowels -o (first person singular), -i- (second and third person singular and the plurals in -mus and -tis) and -u- (third person plural), as in *laudabit*, *habebimus*, *videbunt*. The future of the first and second conjugations thus looks like the imperfect with different vowels: *habebat* ('he was having'), *habebit* ('he will have').

The third and fourth conjugations use a different pattern: they turn the vowel of the present stem into -e- (and -a- in the first person singular), without a b: *mittet*, *credent*, *audiet*, *sciemus*. The fourth conjugation and the third conjugation -io verbs add an i: *audient*, *accipiet*. The first person singular of this pattern ends in -am, which is also the ending of the present subjunctive, so the analyser leaves many such forms undecided and the paradigms below show fewer of them.

sections.heading: Present or future in the third conjugation?
body: In the third conjugation the present and the future of the third person differ by one vowel: *mittit* is present ('he sends'), *mittet* is future ('he will send'); *credit* and *credet*, *ponit* and *ponet*. Read the vowel before the final -t, and in the plural before -nt (*mittunt* against *mittent*).
In the first and second conjugations the b makes the future unmistakable: *dat* (present) against *dabit* (future); *habet* against *habebit*.

sections.heading: Reading the tenses in a sentence
body: In John 13:7 the two tenses stand next to each other: *tu nescis modo: scies autem postea*. The present *nescis* tells what is true now, the future *scies* what will be true afterwards; the adverbs point the same way.

A future in the Vulgate can also state a command or a promise: *videbitis* is often better rendered 'you will see' than 'you shall see'. English 'shall' and 'will' carry meanings Latin does not mark, so use the plain future when you translate.

misunderstandings: -ba- is not the whole of the imperfect: the vowel before it differs by conjugation. *habebat* and *audiebat* are both imperfect, but only the second has -ie-.
The future endings -bit and -bunt do not appear in the third and fourth conjugations. A form such as *mittet* has no b, yet it is a future; do not read it as a present because the b is missing.
The imperfect does not mean that the action was long. It shows how the speaker looks at the action (as going on, repeated or customary), not how long it lasted.
Latin has no auxiliary 'will' or 'would': the future and imperfect forms are single words, and *habebit* means 'he will have' even though English needs two words.

deeper.heading: Where -ba- and -bo come from
body: The origin of the -ba- imperfect and the -bo future is disputed. One common view connects the -b- with the root of *fui*, 'I was', so that -ba- would once have meant something like 'was' added to the stem; other accounts differ on the details. For the learner it is enough that the signs are fixed and regular.

examples.analysis: Four imperfects in a row describe Herod's habit towards John. *metuebat* (*metuo*, third conjugation) is 'he feared'; *custodiebat* (*custodio*, fourth conjugation) 'he kept him safe'; *faciebat* (*facio*) 'he did'; *audiebat* (*audio*) 'he used to listen'. All four are third person singular: the -ba-/-ieba- sign and then -t. The imperfect shows an attitude that lasted and recurred, not a single event.

examples.analysis: *nesciebam* is the first person singular of the imperfect of *nescio*: 'I did not know', or 'I was not knowing'. The ending is -m, not -o, and the sign is -ieba-. The imperfect fits a state of ignorance that lasted until the moment the speaker is describing.

examples.analysis: A present and a future of the same family stand side by side. *nescis* is present: 'you do not know' now. *scies* is the future of *scio*: 'you will know'. It is a fourth-conjugation verb, so the future has -e- and no b, and the ending -s marks the second person singular. The adverbs *modo* and *postea* point the same way.
